lines.note: Feǒxi / fiǒxi qiqi is concerned with hearing or keeping rhythm. The Portuguese begins by calling the person well measured, rather than defining a particular instrument.
The coordinated verbs tanger and bailar specify instrumental performance and dancing. Entoado adds being in tune or suitably coordinated; it continues the preceding person's description.
Feôzǒ / fiôzǒ denotes a representation or image. Figura and moſtra describe something that makes absent events present to view, rather than necessarily a physical statue.

runs.text: ſas paſſadas, ou de couſas que aõ de vir.

lines.note: Both past things and things yet to come can be represented. The printed aõ de vir is the future construction; no modern spelling or accent normalization is needed.
Feqi is heki, here glossed cabe, 'wall'. Feqiuo fedatete begins a Japanese example of separation by a wall; Parede and Vt belong to the Portuguese explanation, not the Japanese phrase.

runs.text: Eſtaua diuidido com parede no meo.

lines.note: Fedatete ita means being separated, with the wall intervening. Portuguese no meo makes the intervening position explicit; the initial te completes the preceding physical line.

This second Feqi is an ailment of the shoulders, not 'wall'. Meliùs recommends Qenbeqi as the preferred term; that distinction makes the OCR's Melnits / Cenbeqi suspect and the scan supports their correction.
Feqiuo vtçu describes striking or patting the affected shoulder area. The Portuguese continues into the next line, so pancadas should not be read as a separate dictionary sense.

runs.text: parte das eſpadoas que doe, ou està leſa.

lines.note: The target is the part of the shoulders that hurts or is injured. This confirms the bodily sense of Feqi rather than the homographic wall entry above.

runs.text: Hum liuro da China de certas medi-

lines.note: Feqigan is identified as a Chinese book of meditations. The wording supports treating it as a title; identifying a particular modern edition would go beyond what this line establishes.
Taçoẽs completes meditaçoẽs from the preceding line. It is a short continuation, not an independent entry or page furniture.
Feqiguiocu corresponds to heki-gyoku, with tama, tama supplying a Japanese gloss for precious stones. The repeated tama is printed and is not removed as an accidental duplication.
Feqira is glossed midorino tçuta, green ivy. Portuguese era here names ivy; it is not the unrelated verb form 'was'.
Viçoſa adds luxuriant or vigorous growth to the ivy description. This brief continuation belongs with the previous line's botanical sense.
Feqiracu refers to the sky or air. The scan supports restoring the missing r in the headword and reading ar, rather than the OCR's meaningless dr.
Feqirano ten is another expression for a clear, beautiful sky. Ten is the Sino-Japanese sky/heaven element, while the Portuguese supplies its descriptive qualities.

The headword is indexed as Feqireqi, while Canàximi plainly supplies kanashimi, sorrow. The example wraps after Fe-; its continuation needs special care because its spelling is not a familiar modern phrase.

Feqireqi xǔxǒ ſu describes great pain and grieving. The continuation is qireqi, agreeing with the headword, and the enlarged u carries a caron; the OCR had lost r and misread the marked vowel as i. The Japanese interpretation remains tied to the dictionary's kanashimi gloss.
ſteza completes triſteza. Together with dòr, this confirms that the preceding example concerns grieving rather than the thunder sense that a similar-looking word might suggest.
Feqiri and Feriqiri are equated as names for a partition or division. The next example begins after the paragraph sign and continues across the line break.
Feqiriuo ſuru means making such a partition. The qiri continuation fits both the preceding headword and the scan, unlike the OCR's quri.
The partition is made within a house. Diuiſão is an alternative Portuguese explanation of repartimento, not another Japanese word.

runs.text: Feqiri, u, itta. i, Feriqiriuo ſuru.

lines.note: The verb paradigm Feqiri, u, itta is equated with Feriqiriuo ſuru. The shared gloss explains why the noun and verbal entry appear together.

Feqiriù banjin evokes a sheer wall or cliff of immense height, conventionally 'wall-standing ten thousand fathoms'. NINJAL supports this headword identity; the scan, not that normalized index, governs its printed accent.
Monte ingreme completes the comparison with a steep mountain. This is still the explanation of Feqiriù banjin, not the beginning of the next botanical entry.
This Feqiſǒ is cabeno cuſa, grass growing on a wall. The wall element distinguishes it from the homophonous green-grass entry below.

runs.text: parede de barro que logo ſe ſeca. Tomaſe por

lines.note: The grass grows on an earthen wall and soon dries. Tomaſe por introduces a figurative application rather than another botanical characteristic.

runs.text: couſa breue, & de pouca dura. S.

lines.note: The figurative sense is something short-lived or of little duration. Dura here functions as duration or lastingness, not simply the modern adjective 'hard'.
The second Feqisǒ is midorino cuſa, fresh green grass. The initial is F, not the OCR's r; the printed short s is retained independently of the preceding headword's ſ.
Verdes completes the description of fresh, green plants. It belongs to the second Feqisǒ entry, not the earlier grass that quickly dries.
Feqitai is cabeno coqe, moss on a wall. Coqe reads koke, and the Portuguese Muſgos gives the same identification.
De completes parede. This short line is essential to the preceding definition even though most of its width is blank.
Feqitan is midorino fuchi, a green-looking deep pool. Portuguese pègo names the deep water, not the unrelated verb 'I catch'.

runs.text: parece verde por ſer muito fundo. S.

lines.note: The pool looks green because it is very deep. That causal explanation belongs to the dictionary and should not be replaced with a modern physical explanation of water colour.
Feqiten denotes the sky; Feqitenno xeixucu means the stars or constellations of that sky. Ceo and Vt are Portuguese portions within the otherwise Japanese line.
Eſtrelas do ceo confirms the astronomical reading of xeixucu. The final register label is separate from the Japanese expression.

runs.text: Feqitǒ. Midorino momo. i, Xiroi momo.

lines.note: Feqitǒ is glossed midorino momo and then xiroi momo. The next Portuguese line specifies white blossoms, so xiroi describes the tree's floral variety rather than necessarily its fruit colour.
The definition explicitly says a peach tree with white flowers. Peſegueiro is kept in its printed historical spelling.
Feqixo is a written prohibition posted on paper. The scan supports Proibição, not the OCR's extra b; its association with a wall is completed on the next line.
The notice can be pasted on the wall or hung up. These are alternative ways of displaying the same written prohibition.
Feqixǒ is cabeno vye, the surface of a wall. This differs from both the posted notice above and the green pine below, despite their similar romanization.
Cuchi feqixǒni caqu is followed by Não, continuing a negative explanation. Reading the initial as N matters semantically: the dictionary says the matter cannot be expressed.

runs.text: ſe pode dizer nem explicar. S.

lines.note: The phrase is explained as something one cannot say or explain. I preserve the dictionary's idiomatic interpretation rather than forcing a literal reading of writing a mouth on a wall.
Feqixô is midorino matçu, a green pine. This is the pine sense rather than Feqixǒ, 'on the wall'; the scan's initial F and medial qi also repair substantial OCR corruption.
Freſco supplements verde in the pine description. The short continuation remains attached to the botanical entry.

runs.text: Cana com que amaſſão, & affeiçoão gru-

lines.note: Fera is hera, here a cane implement used to mix and shape paste. The Portuguese gru- continues as grude on the following line.

De completes grude, so the OCR's qe is untenable. Ferauo tçucǒ then begins an idiom about finding an excuse, continued in column 2. The worn c is read with the Japanese tsukau construction; this is a context-assisted reading, not a claim that the damaged letter is unambiguous.

runs.text: occaſião, ou achaque pera deixar a obra que

lines.note: Occaſião or achaque is a pretext for abandoning work. This continues the last Japanese example in column 1, not a new entry at the top of column 2.
The work has been entrusted to the person: encarregada supplies that meaning and the doubled r is visible. Alicubi limits the usage; a new Fera example then starts after the paragraph sign.
Ferauo faru is explained as committing adultery. This is a distinct idiom from the preceding excuse for leaving work; the final X is a usage label, not Japanese text.
Feraxi gives herashi/herasu, decreasing or consuming something. The transitive sense contrasts with Feri, 'to diminish', further down the column.
Ninjuuo feraſu means reducing the number of people. The following Fi- starts another example, not the Portuguese sentence.
Fitouo feraſu is explained as disparaging another person. Ajuntaſe introduces the verb's productive use after other verbal stems.

runs.text: às raizes de alguns verbos. Vt,

lines.note: The Portuguese explicitly refers to roots of verbs; verhos was an OCR error for verbos. Monouo begins an example of this compound construction.
Monouo cui feraſu means using up food by eating it. The next compound begins with Ta-, completed as tacara, riches, on the next line.
Tacarauo tçucai feraſu means spending down wealth. The Portuguese must be Gaſtar, 'spend', and the scan supports that reading rather than Guſtar.
Cuſuriuo xenji feraſu describes reducing medicine by boiling. Cozendo introduces the process; me- continues as mezinhas, remedies.
The water is made to diminish as the medicines boil. This completes the decoction example, not a general instruction for preparing every medicine.
Feri is heri, a border or hem on clothing. The scan's F and the hemming example below distinguish it from the OCR's Peri.

runs.text: Botar debrum, ou a buainhar al-

lines.note: Feriuo toru means adding a border or hemming something. Riuo completes the preceding Fe-; the OCR's ritio does not fit either the printed strokes or the Japanese object phrase.
Clothing and a cap are examples of things that can be hemmed. Tatamino feri- introduces the border of a tatami mat.
Tatamino feriuo tçuquru means making or fitting the mat border. Tatami inside the Portuguese explanation is an embedded Japanese noun whose typeface can be reviewed independently.
This Feri is the intransitive verb heru, to decrease. Etta is its contracted past form; it should not be confused with the earlier noun heri, 'border'.
Mizzuga fetta means that the water decreased. The apparent i in zugaifetta was a segmentation error; the scan reads the particle ga followed by fetta.
Fericudari is the noun for humility, corresponding to herikudari. The separate verb immediately below confirms the noun/verb distinction.
Fericudari, u, atta supplies the verbal paradigm for humbling oneself. The Portuguese reflexive ending in Humilharſe expresses the same relationship.
Feriſaxi is referred to the preferred form vſuberi. The definition begins a kind of mat and continues with its lining on the next line.
Com forro specifies that the mats are lined. The short continuation completes eſteiras across the physical break.
Feritçuqe receives Idem, referring back to the lined-mat definition. It should not acquire a new invented gloss merely because it has its own headword line.
Feſaqi is hesaki, a ship's prow or projecting bow. This is an ordinary Japanese lexical s, irrespective of whether the source uses a long or short glyph.
Feſo is heso, the navel. The example extends that shape metaphor to an iron vessel's projecting part; quanſu is a vessel name rather than a Portuguese word.

runs.text: Remate que tem as panellas de ferro

lines.note: The vessel's feſo is a finishing projection on iron pots. The location, at the bottom, is supplied by the next physical line.
The entry then gives Iacǒno feſo / foſo, the musk pouch. The alternate vowel is explicitly recorded and should not be normalized to only heso.
Papo dalmiſcre completes the musk-pouch definition. The historical almiſcre spelling is supported by the scan; it is not a reason to modernize the text to almíscar.
Feſono vo / foſono vo denotes the umbilical cord. The printed long s, not t, makes the connection with the preceding navel entry explicit.
The Portuguese locates the cord at the child's navel. Feſono vouo qi- begins a Japanese example with vo as the noun 'cord' and uo as its following object particle.
Qiru and tçugu are given as alternatives for cutting the cord here. The intervening l is an alternative marker, not part of a word lotçugu.

runs.text: Fulugem que eſtà pegada na panella de

lines.note: Feſubi names soot adhering to an iron pot. The initial lexical reading is hesubi, not the OCR's helubi; the next line supplies a regional synonym.
The dictionary gives Nabeſumi as the Cami-region term. Cami and Nabeſumi are Japanese material inside the Portuguese explanation; the final X of the previous sense is a label, not Y.

runs.text: Borda do mar, ou de outra couſa. ¶

lines.note: Feta here means an edge or border, including the seashore. Its nautical example continues after Fe- on the next line.
Fetauo noru means sailing along the land or coast. The Portuguese explains a coastal course, not simply boarding a boat.

runs.text: ¶ Itẽ, Aquella folha que eſta pegadano pè,

lines.note: Itẽ introduces another sense: the leaf-like calyx attached to the fruit. The text's reference to its pè describes the attachment point; it is not a human foot.

runs.text: ou parte inferior dos figos de Iapão. ¶

lines.note: The dictionary calls the fruit figos de Iapão and places this part at its lower end. Inferior repairs the OCR's infertor without changing the source's historical fruit terminology.

runs.text: Tirar eſta folha, ou caſca dos

lines.note: Fetauo toru means removing the calyx or outer covering. This example belongs to the fruit sense, not the earlier coast sense.
Figos completes the object of the preceding Portuguese sentence. It remains body text despite the exceptionally short physical line.
This Feta is heta, unskilled or clumsy. It is a different lexical sense from edge and calyx, and the Portuguese Deſengenhoſo / chambão makes that contrast clear.
Fetafetato / fetato is an adverbial expression for a broad, flat fall or impact. The repeated feta is meaningful; the OCR had misread both the initial F and the internal f.

runs.text: ir, ou daralgũa couſa larga de chãpa. Vt,

lines.note: Ir completes cair from the preceding ca-. The Portuguese describes a broad object striking flat; reading ar would create a spurious word across the physical break.
Fetato tauoruru and tçuqu exemplify falling or making contact in this manner. The F is restored from the scan rather than accepted as an initial r.
Pancada deſta maneira completes the flat-impact explanation. It is the Portuguese continuation of the adverbial examples, not an additional Japanese entry.

Fetano caua describes someone inept or careless. This is the unskilled heta sense, with a further expression involving caua; a precise modern equivalent is less certain than the dictionary's own gloss.
Zelada completes desmazelada, careless or slovenly. The physical split is preserved rather than merging the two printed lines.
Fetçucuxi combines passing or extending with tçucuxi, doing completely. Its first gloss concerns extending all the thread, while Itẽ introduces a second use.

runs.text: Permet. Acabar de paſſar, ou ſofrer traba.

lines.note: The second use is finishing the experience or endurance of hardships. The visible traba. continues across the page in trabalhos; I preserve the printed terminal mark rather than inventing a hyphen.
Catchword anticipating lhos at the start of f186, completing trabalhos across the page turn. Kept as page furniture with its existing stable ID, not a duplicate body line.
